editorial:
The Covered Wagon (1923) is the film that created the template for the Hollywood epic Western. Directed by James Cruze for Famous Players-Lasky â€” the corporation that became Paramount Pictures â€” it stars J. Warren Kerrigan, Lois Wilson, and Ernest Torrence in a dramatization of the 1848 Oregon Trail emigration. Cruze filmed on location in Utah's Millard County desert with a production that assembled roughly 500 wagons and 3,000 extras; the scale was unprecedented. The film grossed an estimated $4 million against an $800,000 budget, becoming one of the top commercial performers of the decade. For contemporary creators it offers extensive authentic footage of covered-wagon caravans, river crossings, large cavalry engagements, and frontier camp life that would cost many millions to recreate â€” all drawn from the public-domain 1923 print.

The rights trap here is the audio track. The Covered Wagon was a silent film and has no original recorded score, but every commercial copy in wide circulation â€” including the 1080p Blu-ray rip hosted on Archive.org â€” carries a modern musical score composed and recorded after the film's own copyright expired. That score is an independent, protected work. A creator who downloads the Archive.org item and uses it with the audio intact is distributing an unlicensed score. The correct path is to strip the audio track before reuse, or to pair the silent images with music that is itself public domain or explicitly licensed. Kino Lorber's restoration print additionally embeds the studio's own copyright claim over the specific scan and color work, so sourcing from a pre-restoration print or using the images in silence removes both exposure points at once.
faq: Can I cut footage from this film into my documentary or commercial project?

Yes â€” the 1923 photographic images are public domain in the United States and carry no copyright restriction. The critical step is to strip any modern audio track before use. Commercial copies, including the Archive.org item, carry a modern score that is not public domain. Use the silent images only, or pair them with separately cleared music.
Does the Kino Lorber restoration create a new copyright over the film?

Kino Lorber's restoration work â€” the specific digital scan, noise reduction, and grading applied to the original nitrate or safety print â€” can support a thin copyright claim in that particular edition as a derivative work. That protection covers Kino's authorship in the restoration, not the underlying 1923 footage. The original photographic content remains public domain; what you should not freely copy is Kino's unique rendering of it.
